context.in_practice: Route 1: the tool re-reads the watched file's full contents several times a second (roughly every 0.1 to 0.25 seconds) and reacts when the contents differ from the last read. It does not rely on the file's last-modified timestamp. That timestamp can stay the same across two quick writes, so it can miss one. Because the contents are compared directly, the tool still notices an edit that leaves the file the same size, and it notices editors that replace the file instead of overwriting it. There is no extra library to install or keep up to date; everything uses what ships with the language. A change can show up up to about a quarter of a second late. If the file is saved and then put back to its exact earlier contents between two checks, nothing is reported, because the contents look unchanged.
context.stakes: Whether `watch` reliably notices every save of a file, including quick back-to-back saves and editors that save by writing a new file and renaming it over the old one, without the user having to install anything extra.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 costs constant small background work and up to about 0.25 s of delay, more so for large files, because the whole file is re-read on every check. In return it needs no added library and is not fooled by timestamps.

plan_why: This question is about how `watch` notices file edits while it runs (polling file bytes, with no watcher library and no mtime checks). The sandbox doesn't allow running `watch`. It also has no way to edit a file while a command is running, or between commands, because files can only be created before the first command. Ordinary commands reconcile at startup with their own mechanism, so they can't show this. And only one route was recorded, so there is no behavioural difference to show.
routes: Poll file bytes with the stdlib every 0.1-0.25 s; no watcher library, no mtime
